Guided Inquiry

1 · The curve at 3000 K

Here is the Planck spectral radiance for a body at T = 3000 K — roughly the tungsten filament of an old incandescent bulb. The shaded strip on the wavelength axis is the visible band (~380–750 nm).

Look at where the peak of the curve sits relative to what your eye can see.

2 · Predict: doubling T

You are about to raise T from 3000 K to 6000 K — roughly a doubling. What happens to the total radiated power?

3 · Now drag the temperature

The Temperature slider is live. Take it from 3000 K to 6000 K and watch two things: the peak marches left (toward blue), and the area under the curve explodes. The readout compares total power to the 3000 K baseline.

Near 5800 K — the surface of the Sun — the peak lands right in the middle of the visible band. That is not a coincidence: our eyes evolved for exactly that spectrum.

4 · Two laws, one curve

The same curve, read three ways:

• Peak obeys Wien: λmax · T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K — it marches left as 1/T (red → white).

• Area obeys Stefan–Boltzmann: P = εσAT⁴ — doubling T gives ×16.

• Shape is Planck's distribution, the parent of both.

Try Surface area: power scales linearly (×2, not ×16). Only temperature has T⁴ leverage.

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

Any hot object glows, and the light it gives off is spread over many wavelengths. The sim draws that spread for an ideal glowing body, a black body, and lets you set its temperature and its surface area. It reports the peak wavelength and the total power radiated.

What you'll learn

  • What Planck's curve B(λ, T) shows and how temperature controls it.
  • How Wien's displacement law and the Stefan–Boltzmann law are two readings of that one curve.
  • How the radiated power depends on temperature T and on surface area A.
The set-up: a hot body, and axes on which the sim draws the spread of its light.

What's on screen

  • Teal curve: B(λ, T) against wavelength from 0 to 3000 nm, with the area beneath it shaded.
  • Yellow dot and label: the peak of the curve, with its wavelength λpeak.
  • Coloured strip under the axis: the visible band, 380 to 750 nm.
  • Colour of the glow and Readouts in the sidebar.
See itStart at T = 3000 K and A = 1 m², the opening values. Watch for: the teal curve over the 0 to 3000 nm axis, and the yellow λpeak label on it.

03

A hot body emits a spectrum set by its temperature

A black body absorbs all the radiation that falls on it, and it is also the best possible emitter. The light it gives off is a continuous spread of wavelengths, and the spread depends only on its temperature T, not on what the body is made of. Planck's law gives the spectral radiance:

B(λ, T) = (2hc² / λ⁵) · 1 / (ehc/(λkBT) − 1)
B is the power emitted per unit area, per unit solid angle, per unit wavelength.

The curve is smooth with a single peak. It climbs steeply on the short-wavelength side, reaches its maximum, and then falls away in a long tail toward long wavelengths. Planck's law is the parent of the two simpler laws that follow, because one is read from where the peak sits and the other from the area under the curve.

04

The peak wavelength is set by 1/T

Setting the slope of Planck's curve to zero gives Wien's displacement law. The peak wavelength is inversely proportional to the temperature:

λmax T = b = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K
A hotter body peaks at a shorter wavelength.
T (K)λpeak (nm)where it falls
10002898infrared
3000966infrared, past the 750 nm red edge
5800500middle of the visible band
8000362ultraviolet, below 380 nm

The peak lies in the visible band only for T between about 3900 K and 7600 K. A 3000 K body still glows orange because the curve's tail reaches into the visible, which holds about 11 % of the power.

See itSet T = 5800 K. Watch for: the peak dot inside the coloured strip, with λpeak = 500 nm, and the colour white.
05

Radiated power grows as T⁴

Adding up Planck's curve over every wavelength gives the total power radiated by a surface of area A. This is the Stefan–Boltzmann law:

P = ε σ A T⁴, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/(m²·K⁴)
The sim uses ε = 1, the ideal black body.

At T = 3000 K and A = 1 m² the power is 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 3000⁴ = 4.59 MW. Because P depends on T⁴, doubling T multiplies P by 2⁴ = 16, so 6000 K gives 73.5 MW. Halving T would cut P by 16. The area under the curve grows by the same factor, even though the axis rescales and the curve may look similar in height.

See itDouble T from 3000 K to 6000 K with A = 1 m². Watch for: Radiated power P 73.49 MW and the ratio readout 16.00 ×.
06

Power scales linearly with area

In P = εσAT⁴ the area appears to the first power. Each square metre of surface radiates the same power per second at a given T, so twice the area radiates twice the power. At 3000 K the power is 0.459 MW for 0.1 m², 4.59 MW for 1 m², 9.19 MW for 2 m² and 22.97 MW for 5 m².

Only temperature has the T⁴ leverage. Area does not touch the shape of the curve at all, so λpeak stays put. The ratio readout compares the power with a 3000 K body of the same area, so it does not change when you move the area slider.

See itKeep T = 3000 K and set A = 2 m². Watch for: P 9.19 MW, double the 4.59 MW at 1 m², with the peak still at 966 nm.
07

Where it matters

  • Light bulbs. A filament near 3000 K peaks in the infrared, and only about 11 % of its power is visible light. The rest is heat.
  • Stars. A star's colour gives its surface temperature through Wien's law. The Sun, at about 5800 K, peaks near 500 nm.
  • Thermal cameras. Room-temperature objects peak around 10 000 nm, so cameras detect far infrared to measure temperature.
  • Real surfaces. A real body radiates ε σ A T⁴ with ε below 1, and it also absorbs from its surroundings, so the net loss is εσA(T⁴ − T₀⁴).
08

Summary

In one line. A black body's temperature fixes the whole curve of its light, and the temperature and surface area together fix the power it radiates.

Key points

  • Planck's law gives the curve B(λ, T).
  • Wien: λmax T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K, read from the peak.
  • Stefan–Boltzmann: P = εσAT⁴, read from the area, so doubling T gives ×16.

Common mix-ups

  • "A hotter body radiates more only at its peak." It radiates more at every wavelength, and the total grows as T⁴.
  • "A body that looks red radiates only red light." Its light spans many wavelengths, and the colour is the net effect of the visible part.
  • "Doubling the area gives ×16 as well." Power is linear in A. Only T carries the fourth power.

Things to try on your own

  • Find the temperature at which the peak first enters the visible band, and compare with 2.898 × 10⁻³ ÷ 750 × 10⁻⁹.
  • Predict the power at T = 4500 K and A = 1 m², then check it. It is 5.06 times the 3000 K value.
  • Find an area and a temperature that radiate the same power as 1 m² at 3000 K.
